evidence: Cels. 4.1.3: alterum asperam artēriam nōminant, alterum stomachum
Cic. ND 2.136: aspera artēria (sīc enim ā medicīs appellātur)
terms.comment: The physicians’ name, as Cicero says, and Celsus’s: the “rough artery”, rough on its outer side, where it is made of rings (Cels. 4.1.3), as against from the arteries of the blood (see artery). It renders Greek τραχεῖα ἀρτηρία, from which the anatomists’ term Trachea (Terminologia Anatomica) comes; Macrobius’s trāchīa (Sat. 7.15, Lewis & Short) is late and rare.

terms.gloss: the windpipe; often plural in this sense
evidence: Plin. NH 11.175–176: interior earum appellātur artēria, ad pulmōnem atque cor pertinēns
terms.comment: The windpipe is the word’s first sense in Lewis & Short; in the plural, of its two parts, in the Rhetorica ad Herennium and Suetonius (Lewis & Short). It is also an artery, so where it might be taken so, aspera artēria is plainer.

phrases.latin: Deinde duo itinera incipiunt: alterum asperam artēriam nōminant, alterum stomachum.
phrases.english: Then two passages begin: one they call the windpipe, the other the gullet.

sources: Lewis & Short: arteria · Lewis & Short: trachia
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 59, 407.
